section.title: John's Question and Come to Me
section.sectionRationale: The chapter gathers responses to Jesus. John, imprisoned and perplexed, sends to ask if Jesus is really the Coming One; Jesus points to His works and honors John as more than a prophet. He rebukes a fickle generation that rejected both John and Himself, pronounces woe on unrepentant cities that saw His miracles, and then, astonishingly, praises the Father and issues the gentlest invitation in the Gospels: come to Me and find rest.
section.thesis: Jesus answers doubt with the evidence of His messianic works, exposes the hardness of a generation that will receive neither John nor Him, warns the privileged but unrepentant of judgment, and reveals Himself as the Son who alone knows the Father and who welcomes the weary with the offer of rest under His gentle yoke.
section.frameNote: Five beats: John's question and Jesus' answer; Jesus' testimony about John; the fickle generation; woe to the unrepentant cities; and the Father revealed to little children and the invitation to rest.

verses.text: After Jesus had finished instructing His twelve disciples, He went on from there to teach and preach in their cities.
Meanwhile John heard in prison about the works of Christ, and he sent his disciples
to ask Him, “Are You {{erchomenos|the One who was to come}}, or should we look for someone else?”
Jesus replied, “Go back and report to John what you hear and see:
The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor.
Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.”

units.label: More than a prophet
units.note: the Elijah who was to come

verses.text: As John’s disciples were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind?
Otherwise, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? Look, those who wear fine clothing are found in kings’ palaces.
What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You.’
Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has risen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has been subject to violence, and the violent lay claim to it.
For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John.
And if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come.
He who has ears, let him hear.

units.label: This generation
units.note: wisdom is vindicated by her actions

verses.text: To what can I compare this generation? They are like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling out to others:
‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’
For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon!’
The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ But wisdom is vindicated by her actions.”

units.label: Woe to the unrepentant
units.note: the cities that saw His miracles

verses.text: Then Jesus began to denounce the cities in which most of His miracles had been performed, because they did not repent.
“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.

And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Sodom, it would have remained to this day.
But I tell you that it will be more bearable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”
At that time Jesus declared, “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children.
Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight.
All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.
Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you {{anapauo|rest}}.
Take My {{zygos|yoke}} upon you and learn from Me, for I am {{praus|gentle}} and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.”

erchomenos.gloss: The Coming One, a title for the awaited Messiah. John asks whether Jesus is truly the promised deliverer; Jesus answers not with a claim but with the works Isaiah foretold the Messiah would do.

anapauo.gloss: To give rest, refresh, relieve. Jesus promises rest to the weary and heavy-laden, the deep relief of a soul brought to Him; it echoes the Sabbath rest and the rest God gives His people, now found in the Son.

zygos.gloss: Yoke, the wooden frame joining oxen for work, a common image for the burden of the law or a teacher's discipline. Jesus offers His own yoke, His gracious rule and teaching, which, unlike the crushing yoke of the scribes, is easy and light.

praus.gloss: Gentle, meek, humble. Jesus describes His own heart as gentle and lowly, the only place in the Gospels where He tells us what He is like within; it is the ground of His invitation, a Savior tender toward the weary.

basic.context: John the Baptist, now in prison, sends to ask whether Jesus is really the promised Messiah. Jesus answers by pointing to His works, the very things Isaiah said the Messiah would do. He praises John as more than a prophet, the promised Elijah, yet says the least in the kingdom is greater. He rebukes a generation that rejected both John's austerity and His own openness, warns the cities that saw His miracles but did not repent, and then invites the weary to come to Him for rest.
basic.hermeneutics: Read John's question with sympathy: even the greatest prophet can struggle when Jesus does not act as expected. Jesus' answer teaches us to test His identity by His works and words fulfilling Scripture. The chapter then sets human hardness against divine grace, ending not in condemnation but in the tenderest invitation, revealing the heart of Christ toward the burdened.
basic.originalLanguages: John asks if Jesus is the Coming One, the awaited Messiah. Jesus offers rest, deep relief, to the weary. He speaks of His yoke, the frame that joins oxen for work, a picture of a teacher's rule, but His is easy. And He describes His own heart as gentle and humble, the one place He tells us what He is like within.
basic.typology: Jesus' works fulfill Isaiah's portrait of the age of salvation, when the blind see and the poor hear good news. John fulfills Malachi's promised messenger and Elijah. And the rest Jesus gives fulfills the Sabbath rest and the rest promised to God's people, now found in the Son rather than in the law.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Coming One whose works prove His identity, the Son who alone knows the Father and reveals Him, and the gentle and lowly Savior who invites the weary to rest. His self-description, gentle and humble in heart, is the tender center of the Gospel: the Lord of heaven and earth is approachable, kind, and easy to come to.
basic.god: The Father is Lord of heaven and earth, sovereign in hiding truth from the self-sufficient and revealing it to the childlike. He is well pleased to save the humble. And He has entrusted all things to the Son, so that He is known only through Him. Grace, not human cleverness, opens the door to knowing God.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 35 and 61 describe the messianic works Jesus lists. Malachi 3 and 4 promise the messenger and Elijah. Jeremiah 6 offers rest for your souls to those who walk in the good way. And 1 Corinthians 1 says God hides wisdom from the wise and reveals it to the lowly.
basic.oneStory: Faced with doubt, rejection, and hardness, Jesus does not withdraw the offer of grace but extends it more warmly than ever. He is the Messiah whose works fulfill Scripture, the Son who reveals the Father, and the gentle Lord who calls the weary to rest. The chapter moves from John's honest question through the world's stubbornness to the open arms of Christ: come to Me, and I will give you rest.

context.literary:
Chapter 11 follows the mission discourse and is built like a staircase that climbs in a single direction: the closer people are to Jesus, the more is asked of them. It opens with a question from John in prison, passes to a long defence of John before the crowds, moves to a judgment on the generation that heard both of them and on three cities, and ends in a prayer and an invitation. The pivot is verse 25, marked by the words at that time, and by it the tone changes from rebuke to tenderness without any break in the thought. The woes of verses 20 to 24 and the invitation of verses 28 to 30 are not two moods but two halves of one appeal.

The passage is also a chain of questions. John asks one in verse 3, and Jesus answers with three of His own in verses 7 to 9, each beginning with the same words, what did you go out to see? The repetition makes the crowd answer for itself: not a reed, not a courtier, but a prophet. In verse 16 He asks another, to what can I compare this generation? and answers it with a children's game. The one who is asked about His identity turns the questions back on the questioners.

A hidden unity runs through the units. John did not behave as people expected and neither did Jesus; both were rejected, and the unit about the children in the marketplace says why. The woes about the cities say what the rejection costs, and the prayer in verses 25 to 27 says who sees through it: not the clever but the infants. The invitation then offers rest to the very people the clever have overlooked.

Verse 11:1 also marks the end of the discourse and begins a new movement that runs to chapter 12, in which Jesus is increasingly opposed. Chapter 11 is the doorway, where the reception of Jesus becomes the question that divides the audience, and where His answer is not an argument but a summons.
context.historical:
John had been arrested by Herod Antipas, whom he had publicly rebuked for taking his brother Philip's wife, Matthew 14:3-4. Imprisonment under a ruler who wanted him dead, and was held back only by fear of the crowd, Matthew 14:5, makes the question of verse 3 more human. A man who had cried out that the axe lay at the root of the trees, Matthew 3:10, and that a Coming One would clear the threshing floor with fire, Matthew 3:12, now sat in a cell while the Coming One healed the blind and ate with tax collectors. The mismatch was not one of faith in God but of expectation about how the day of the LORD would arrive.

The reply of Jesus is built from Isaiah. The blind see, the deaf hear and the mute shout in Isaiah 35:5-6, and the poor hear good news in Isaiah 61:1. Isaiah 29:18 also puts the deaf hearing and the blind seeing among the signs of the coming day. Jesus adds the cleansing of lepers and the raising of the dead, two wonders He has just shown in chapters 8 and 9, and so gathers all that He has been doing under the signs of Isaiah's day. By answering with Scripture, He tells John to read the situation by the prophets, not by the sword.

The crowd's memory of John was vivid. He had lived in the wilderness, wearing camel's hair and eating locusts and wild honey, Mark 1:6, and large crowds had gone out to him. A reed swaying in the wind and a man in fine clothes were two familiar contrasts: the first a picture of an unstable man, the second a picture of a court preacher who would flatter the powerful. John was neither. His austere clothing and his fate in prison showed that he was a prophet of the old kind.

The three cities of verses 20 to 24 sat on or near the north shore of the Sea of Galilee and were the centre of much of Jesus' Galilean ministry. Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician coastal cities that the prophets had condemned for pride, and Sodom had become the proverbial example of judgment, Genesis 19:24-28. To say that these pagan cities would have repented is to say that the Galilean towns were worse off than Israel's old enemies.

The yoke of verse 29 was an everyday object and a common picture. A yoke joined two animals for work, and in Jewish teaching it was a figure for submitting to Torah, to a teacher, or to a ruler. Jeremiah 27:11 speaks of putting the neck under the yoke of a king. In the language of the day, to take a teacher's yoke was to become his disciple.
context.canonical:
John's story is stitched into the prophets at two points. Malachi 3:1 promised a messenger who would prepare the way before the LORD, and Jesus quotes that verse in 11:10 with a small change that puts the way before Jesus Himself. Malachi 4:5-6 promised Elijah before the great and awesome day of the LORD, and Jesus says in verse 14 that John is that Elijah, a reading He repeats in Matthew 17:10-13 and that Luke 1:17 sets out when it says John goes before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. Yet in John 1:21 the Baptist himself denies being Elijah, which shows that the identification is a statement about his role in God's plan rather than a claim about who he took himself to be.

The works that Jesus lists in verse 5 are the signs by which Isaiah recognised the coming of God. Isaiah 35:4 says that God Himself will come to save, and the next verses give the miracles. Isaiah 61:1-2 is the passage Jesus reads in the synagogue of Nazareth and says is fulfilled in their hearing, Luke 4:18-21. The works of verse 5 are therefore not only evidence that He is the Messiah; they are evidence that the day of the LORD has begun in the person of Jesus.

The woes against Capernaum draw on Isaiah 14:13-15, where the king of Babylon says in his heart that he will ascend to the heavens and is brought down to Sheol. Jesus' question, will you be lifted up to heaven? borrows the king's language and turns it on a Galilean town. The comparison with Sodom ties Capernaum to the old story of judgment and gives the verse its force, and the same pattern is used in Matthew 12:41-42, where the men of Nineveh and the Queen of the South will rise to condemn this generation.

The invitation of verses 28 to 30 draws on the long thread of rest in the Bible. Exodus 33:14 records the LORD promising Moses that His presence will go with him and give him rest. Jeremiah 6:16 calls the people to the ancient paths with the promise of rest for their souls, and Matthew 11:29 repeats the phrase nearly word for word. Psalm 62:1 says that in God alone the soul finds rest. Hebrews 4:9-10 later takes up the same theme and says that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God. The gentleness of Jesus echoes the prophet Zechariah's king, who comes humble, Zechariah 9:9, a text Matthew quotes at the entry into Jerusalem. And the praise of the Father for revealing His things to infants is paralleled in Luke 10:21-22 and in Paul's argument that God chose the lowly things of the world, 1 Corinthians 1:26-29.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew places this chapter after the mission discourse so that the reader sees a reaction to Jesus that cannot be avoided. His aim is to answer a question the early church could not escape: why did the Messiah meet so much doubt, even from the best of men, and so much hostility from the many? The answer he gives is not that Jesus failed to make His case. Jesus pointed to the works that the prophets had foretold. The trouble lay in the hearers, who wanted the Messiah and His forerunner to fit their own pattern, and who found a reason to reject each whichever way they came.

He also means to protect the honour of John. A reader might suppose that John's question was a failure of nerve. Matthew lets Jesus answer it with kindness and then praise John in front of the crowd. The greatest of the prophets is not diminished by a moment of struggle in prison. Matthew wants readers who are suffering or doubting to see that they are not cast out, and that Jesus answers questions put honestly.

Most of all, the author brings the reader to the invitation. The woes are meant to be heard against it, and the rest is meant to be heard as an offer to people who know that they have laboured and have not arrived. Verse 27 is the foundation for it, since only the Son knows the Father and can therefore offer what the Father holds. The author intends the hearer to come away knowing that there is a person to go to, and that the going is not a matter of cleverness but of coming.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
John's question is recorded, not commanded. The passage does not tell believers to question Jesus whenever the facts are hard, but it shows what Jesus does when someone does, and it permits honest wrestling with the way the kingdom comes. The commendation of John comes after the question, not before, so doubt is not blamed. What is commanded is the response that follows: do not fall away on account of Me, verse 6, and that is the abiding instruction.

The denunciation of the cities describes a judgment that fell on particular towns and speaks of a degree of responsibility proportioned to privilege. It does not set a rule for ranking sins, and it does not give a licence to condemn other towns today. It warns that those who have seen the most are accountable for the most, which should be heard as a challenge to settled churches before it is heard as a verdict on others.

The invitation is the plain prescription. Come, take, learn: all three verbs are imperatives given to everyone who is weary and burdened. They do not wait on a qualification, and they apply directly to hearers today. The yoke, however, is not a promise of a life without obligation. Jesus does not say there is no yoke; He says that His is easy and that learning from Him is the way to rest. The passage should not be read as permission to ignore His commands, nor as a recipe for relief from every kind of suffering, since the same Gospel has just warned of persecution. It promises rest for the soul, and the rest is found in submission to Him, not apart from it.

debates.question: Why did John, the great forerunner, come to doubt?

views.label: Genuine perplexity from prison
views.case: John had announced a mighty Judge with a winnowing fork, yet from a cell he heard of a gentle healer; the gap between expectation and reality, sharpened by suffering, prompted his honest question.

views.label: Asking for his disciples' sake
views.case: Some hold John sent his followers less for himself than to have their own doubts answered directly by Jesus, redirecting them to the Messiah as his own ministry closed.

debates.bearing: Either way Jesus responds with gentle reassurance and pronounces a blessing on those who do not stumble over Him, treating honest doubt with tenderness, not rebuke.

debates.question: What does it mean that the kingdom suffers violence and the violent lay claim to it?

views.label: The kingdom is violently opposed
views.case: From John's imprisonment onward, violent people, like Herod, attack the kingdom and its heralds, so the saying describes the hostility the kingdom meets as it advances.

views.label: The kingdom is forcefully advancing and seized by the earnest
views.case: The alternative rendering takes it positively: the kingdom presses forward with power, and those who are in earnest lay hold of it with wholehearted determination.

debates.bearing: Both fit the context of division: the kingdom meets fierce opposition, yet it advances, and it must be entered by those who press in against the resistance.

debates.question: What does it mean that the least in the kingdom is greater than John?

views.label: A difference of position in the story of salvation
views.case: John stands at the end of the old order, the last of the Prophets and the Law, verse 13, and sees the Messiah but not the cross and resurrection. Even the humblest believer, living after them, has a place in the kingdom that John did not yet enter. The comparison is about era and privilege, not about worth or character.

views.label: A statement about those who belong to Jesus
views.case: The one who is least in the kingdom has the forgiveness and the Spirit that are the gift of the kingdom, and these exceed what even a great prophet had before Jesus' work was done. The greatness is the kingdom's, not the person's.

debates.bearing: Both views honour John as the greatest of the old order and put the weight of greatness on the new thing God is doing in Christ, so that no believer should think of himself as small when he stands in what Jesus has brought.

study.originalLanguages:
John's question in verse 3 is put in terms of ho erchomenos, the Coming One. The participle is a title in the making. Psalm 118:26 says, blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD, and the crowd shouts this of Jesus at the entry into Jerusalem, Matthew 21:9. John's question asks whether Jesus is the one the psalm and the prophets pointed to, or whether another is to be expected. The verb that follows, prosdokao, to look for or wait for, belongs to the language of expectation. The question is about whether the waiting is over.

Verse 2 says that John heard of the works of the Christ. Matthew's own word here, in the narrator's voice, is Christos, Messiah, and he attaches it to the works of Jesus, ta erga. The works, not a claim, are what define the Messiah in the eyes of the prisoner. Jesus replies with the same word, go and report, apangeilate, and the report is about what is heard and seen, the two senses that carry testimony.

The blessing in verse 6 is addressed to the one who does not skandalizo, who is not tripped up or made to stumble. The Greek noun skandalon means a trap or a stumbling block, and the verb is the one Jesus uses elsewhere of those who fall away under pressure, Matthew 13:21. The gentleness of the verse is in its form: Jesus does not accuse John of stumbling, He gives a beatitude to the one who does not.

In verse 12 the verb is biazetai, which can be read as middle or passive, the kingdom either forces its way forward or suffers violence, and the next clause names biastai, violent or forceful men, who harpazo, seize or snatch it. The ambiguity is real and the debate above reflects it. Whatever the reading, the vocabulary of force and seizure describes a kingdom that does not advance quietly.

In verse 25 Jesus says exomologoumai, I praise or openly acknowledge You. The verb is the same one Matthew uses of confessing sins at John's baptism in 3:6, so the word that covered public admission of sin also covers public acknowledgment of God. The infants for whom the Father has revealed these things are nepioi, a word for babies or very young children, in contrast to the sophoi and synetoi, the wise and the learned. The Father's reason is stated as eudokia, good pleasure or favourable will: it was well pleasing in His sight. The revealing is not an accident but a choice.

In verse 27 the knowing is epiginosko, a full or thorough knowing, and it is mutual between Father and Son. Between them nothing is left unknown. The Son also has all things paredothe, handed over to Him, and the verb is the same one used of delivering and handing on a tradition, which here describes the Father's entrusting of everything to the Son. Revelation is then the Son's to give, to those whom He wills, and the verb for willing, boulētai, is a word for deliberate purpose.

The invitation of verse 28 addresses those who kopiao and are pephortismenoi, labouring to the point of weariness and loaded with burdens. The two words describe a worker bent under a load. The promised rest is anapauo, a rest that refreshes, which He says in verse 29 will be found by their souls. The same noun, anapausis, is what Jesus promises, and it is not a vacation but the settled peace of a person who has set down the load. The yoke is chrestos, easy, but the adjective means good, kind and well fitted, as a yoke made to the shape of the neck. The two adjectives of verse 29 are praus, gentle, and tapeinos, humble or lowly. Matthew uses praus again of the king who comes to Jerusalem, 21:5, and in the Beatitudes of the meek who inherit the earth, 5:5. It is the one place in Matthew where Jesus says what His own heart is like.

typology.type: John as the messenger of Malachi and the Elijah to come
typology.fulfillment: Malachi 3:1 promised a messenger to prepare the way before the LORD, and Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah before the day of the LORD. Jesus identifies John with both, saying that if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come. John wore a prophet's rough clothing, called a nation to repentance, and confronted a king, as Elijah confronted Ahab, 1 Kings 18:1-4, and like Elijah he was hunted by a ruler's wife. The correspondence is in role and spirit, Luke 1:17, not in identity, as John 1:21 shows. The escalation is that Elijah prepared for the day of the LORD, while John prepared for the Lord in person. The type falls short because John is a forerunner only, and he himself says that Jesus must increase and he must decrease, John 3:30.

typology.type: The works of the Coming One
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 35:5-6 and 61:1 sketched the signs of the day when God would come to save. In the reply to John, Jesus lists those signs as His present activity and adds the raising of the dead. The correspondence is exact: the blind receive sight, the deaf hear, the poor hear good news. The escalation lies in who is doing them. In the prophets God comes to do them; in Matthew the one doing them is Jesus, and Luke 4:18-21 records His own statement that the scripture is fulfilled today. The pattern is not yet complete, since the final removal of all sickness and death waits for the new creation, Revelation 21:4.

The Bible's rest begins with the seventh day, when God rested from His work, Exodus 20:11, and continues in the promise to Moses that the LORD's presence will give rest, Exodus 33:14, and in the rest of the land under Joshua, Hebrews 4:8. Jeremiah 6:16 called the people back to the good way where they would find rest for their souls. Jesus offers that rest in His own person and in the learning that comes from Him. The correspondence is the rest God Himself enjoys and shares; the escalation is that it is found by coming to a person. Hebrews 4:9-10 says that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, so the type is both fulfilled in Christ now and awaiting its fullness.

In Jewish usage the yoke stood for submission to God's law or to a teacher's instruction, and the Pharisees were accused of laying heavy loads on people's shoulders, Matthew 23:4. The Jerusalem council later says that the yoke of the law was one that neither they nor their fathers could bear, Acts 15:10. Jesus does not abolish the idea of a yoke; He offers His own, which is light because He carries it with the disciple and because it is shaped by gentleness. Paul says Christ has set us free so that we should not be burdened again with a yoke of slavery, Galatians 5:1, and John says the commandments are not burdensome, 1 John 5:3. The type falls short only if the yoke is thought of as a burden to be earned rather than a relationship to be entered.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ by what Jesus will and will not do with the titles offered to Him. John asks whether He is the Coming One, and Jesus does not say yes or no. He lets the works answer. The result is a model of how the Gospel presents Him: His identity is shown in what He does and gathered from what the Scriptures said He would do. By the time the reader reaches verse 5, the lists of Isaiah 35 and 61 have been matched with the miracles of chapters 8 and 9, and the claim is made without a single self-description. Luke 4:18-21 shows that Jesus knew the passage He was fulfilling.

The beatitude in verse 6 is one of the most personal lines in the Gospel. Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me. It does not say, on account of the kingdom, or the law, but of Me. The blessing attaches to a person, and what is at stake is whether people will trust Him when He does not behave as they expect. The point is sharpened by what follows: the Baptist had spoken of fire and a winnowing fork, Matthew 3:12, and the Messiah arrives with a healing hand and a table. Jesus asks John, and every later reader, to hold on to Him even when He disappoints expectation.

He also stands as the one who is greater than the greatest. The comparison with John is not an insult but a measure: John is the best of the old order and Jesus brings the new, and in Matthew 12:41-42 He says that one greater than Jonah and one greater than Solomon is here. His own account of John makes sense only because He is the one for whom John prepared the way, Malachi 3:1.

The prayer and invitation of verses 25 to 30 show the heart of His identity. The Father has handed everything to the Son, John 3:35, and only the Son knows the Father fully, so that to see Him is to see the Father, John 14:9. This is the claim the Gospel makes in its boldest form: He is the exclusive revealer. And what He reveals is a Father whose pleasure it is to make Himself known to infants. The Son is not a barrier between us and God but the way through, and John 1:18 says that the one and only Son has made the Father known.

Then the lines of power and tenderness are drawn together. The one to whom all things are given is the one who is gentle and humble in heart. He does not offer rest by lecture but by presence, and the word learn from Me makes Him the teacher whose own character is the curriculum. This is the Messiah of Zechariah 9:9, righteous and victorious but humble, and the Servant who will not break a bruised reed, as chapter 12 will show. Moses was the most humble man on earth, Numbers 12:3, but Moses never said, come to me. Only the one who bears the name of the Lord can say it.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The yoke is not a coded picture of the cross, and the infants are not a riddle about specific people. The links above rest on the claims Jesus makes here and on how the New Testament elsewhere takes them up, for example in John 6:37, where He promises never to drive away the one who comes to Him.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is first of all the Father who reveals. Verses 25 and 26 are a prayer, and they show that revelation is God's act and His choice. He hides and He reveals, and He does it because it is well pleasing to Him. This is not arbitrary in a way that makes God cruel; it humbles every human claim to have worked out the truth. The wise and learned are not condemned for being intelligent, but the same pride that rested on its own insight is what prevents them from receiving. Paul draws the same conclusion when he says that God chose the lowly so that no one may boast in His presence, 1 Corinthians 1:26-29. In this passage God is Lord of heaven and earth, and the title is chosen to show that no human mind or institution stands beyond His rule.

He is a God who is patient with doubt. John's question is not turned away, and the answer comes from the Lord Himself with the evidence of Scripture and a gentle word at the end. This is an aspect of the character of God that the rest of the Bible confirms: He deals kindly with those who struggle. Thomas is given what he asked for in John 20:27, and the father of the sick boy hears the honest cry, I do believe; help my unbelief, Mark 9:24. The God of this chapter is not threatened by honest questions.

He is also a God who judges with proportion. The woes on the cities are not random. They are tied to the amount of light given: the miracles done in them, if done elsewhere, would have produced repentance. Judgment is measured by privilege, and there are degrees on the day of judgment. This does not weaken the judgment but gives it its justice. It also stands next to verse 28 as its dark side. The God who calls the weary is the God who holds the unrepentant to account, and both come from the same Lord.

The inner life of God is opened in verse 27. Father and Son know each other in a way no outsider can. The Son has received all things, and the Father is known only by the Son's will to reveal Him. This is the doctrine of the Trinity in its Gospel form, not as a puzzle but as the ground of invitation: if the Son knows the Father fully, then to be brought to the Son is to be brought to the Father. John 17:2 and 3:35 say that the Father has given all things into His hands.

He is a God of rest. The Sabbath and the promises of rest that run through the Old Testament show that God's own character is one of settled peace, and that He wishes His people to share it. The rest offered by Jesus is not escape from God but entry into His own rest, Hebrews 4:10.

For worship, this chapter asks us to pray as Jesus prays, with open thanks that the Father hides things from the proud and gives them to the childlike, and to come to Him without any pretence of being sorted out. It asks us to treat His invitation as His most characteristic word. The God who reveals Himself and who invites the weary is not a distant lawgiver but a Father whose heart is seen in a gentle and humble Son.

crossReferences.note: The eyes of the blind opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped, the lame leaping and the mute tongue shouting for joy. Jesus lists these as the present works of His ministry in verse 5, so that the signs of the prophet become the evidence offered to a doubting prisoner.

The Spirit-anointed one who preaches good news to the poor and binds up the brokenhearted. The last item in Jesus' list, the good news preached to the poor, comes from here, and Jesus reads the passage in Nazareth as fulfilled in His own ministry, Luke 4:18-21.

God promises to send a messenger to prepare the way before Him. Jesus quotes it in verse 10 and gives it a sharper edge by turning it toward Himself, and so identifies John as the forerunner and Himself as the one the way was prepared for.

Elijah the prophet is promised before the great and awesome Day of the LORD. Jesus says John is that Elijah, if people will accept it, and Matthew 17:10-13 returns to the idea after the Transfiguration. The identification is in role and spirit, and it shows that the day of the LORD has begun.

The parallel to this passage, with the same question, the same answer and the same children in the marketplace, but with added detail about the tax collectors who acknowledged God's justice and the Pharisees who rejected God's purpose. It shows who in the crowd responded to John and who did not.

The king of Babylon says in his heart that he will ascend to the heavens and is brought down to Sheol. Jesus' question to Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? takes the proud king's language and applies it to a town that thought itself secure.

The men of Nineveh and the Queen of the South will rise at the judgment and condemn this generation, because One greater than Jonah and One greater than Solomon is here. It develops the argument of the woes in the same way, comparing the response of outsiders with that of those who have seen more.

The people are told to ask for the ancient paths and walk in the good way, and then they will find rest for their souls. Jesus' promise in verse 29 repeats the phrase almost exactly, and the saying that follows in Jeremiah, we will not walk in it, shows what is at stake in refusing.

The LORD tells Moses that His Presence will go with him and give him rest. The rest in Matthew 11 is of the same kind: it is not first a state of mind but the nearness of God, and Jesus offers it as the Son who brings the Father's presence.

A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and whoever enters that rest also rests from his own work. The writer takes the same theme of rest and applies it to the believer's present and future, which shows how the early church read Jesus' invitation.

The same prayer of thanks that the Father has hidden things from the wise and revealed them to little children, with the same statement about the Son and the Father. Luke places it at the return of the seventy, which shows that the prayer was an overflow of joy at the success of the mission.

Paul says that not many of the Corinthians were wise, powerful or well born, and that God chose the foolish, the weak and the lowly so that no one may boast. It is a commentary on the Father's good pleasure in verses 25 and 26, applied to the actual makeup of the church.

study.oneStory:
The Bible has been waiting for someone to come. From Genesis 3:15 onward there is a promise of a descendant, and from the prophets there is a growing expectation of a Coming One who would do what Israel and her kings could not. When John asks, are You the One who was to come, he is asking whether the whole long hope has arrived. Jesus' answer is that it has, and the proof is in the same pages that created the hope: Isaiah's blind men see, and the poor hear good news. The waiting of the Old Testament is fulfilled in a person.

The passage also holds the old story of the prophets and their rejection. Israel had killed or silenced the prophets who came to call it back, and Elijah had been hunted. John fits that pattern and ends in a cell, and the generation that mocked both his austerity and the Messiah's openness is the generation of the children who will not play. The hardness of the cities has its roots in the hardness of Pharaoh and the people in the wilderness, and Hebrews 3 and 4 use the same warning from Psalm 95 about hearing His voice and not hardening the heart. The question of whether people will receive what God sends is as old as the Garden.

It sets up what follows. Matthew 12 opens straight away with Sabbath controversies, and the rest Jesus has just promised becomes the very subject of dispute. The confrontation with the leaders grows, and the parables of chapter 13 explain why the kingdom is hidden from some and revealed to others, with the same language of mystery given to some and not to others, Matthew 13:11. Paul's statement that none of the rulers of this age understood the hidden wisdom of God, or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory, 1 Corinthians 2:6-10, is the long echo of verse 25.

The story reaches its end in the rest that Jesus offers. The first creation ended with God's rest, the seventh day, and the rest was lost with the Fall. The land of Canaan brought a partial rest, but the writer of Hebrews says that it was not the final one. Jesus gives it now to souls, and in the new creation it will be complete, with no more weeping, no more pain, and the weary finally at home. The gentle and humble Son who invited the burdened is the one who will wipe every tear from their eyes, Revelation 7:17 and 21:4.

quiz.q: How did Jesus answer John's question about whether He was the Coming One?

options.text: By pointing to His works, the blind seeing and the poor hearing good news, as Isaiah foretold.
options.note: Verses 4-5 answer with the messianic works of Isaiah 35 and 61.

options.text: By simply declaring that He was the Messiah.
options.note: He pointed John to the scriptural evidence of His works rather than making a bare claim.

options.text: By rebuking John for his lack of faith.
options.note: Jesus responded gently, blessing those who do not stumble, not rebuking John.

options.text: By refusing to answer the question at all.
options.note: He gave a clear, scriptural answer through His works.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say about John the Baptist?

options.text: He is more than a prophet, the promised Elijah, yet the least in the kingdom is greater than he.
options.note: Verses 9-14 exalt John while showing the surpassing greatness of the kingdom.

options.text: He was the greatest prophet, greater even than those in the kingdom.
options.note: John is supreme among those born of women, but Jesus says the least in the kingdom is greater still.

options.text: He was merely one prophet among many.
options.note: Jesus calls him more than a prophet, the forerunner Elijah, not one among many.

options.text: He had failed in his mission by doubting.
options.note: Jesus honors John highly despite his question, not as a failure.

quiz.q: How did Jesus describe the generation that rejected both John and Himself?

options.text: Like children who would neither dance to the flute nor mourn to the dirge, refusing every approach.
options.note: Verses 16-19 picture their fickle rejection of both John's austerity and Jesus' openness.

options.text: As sincere seekers who simply needed more evidence.
options.note: The opposite; they had ample evidence and still refused, criticizing whatever came.

options.text: As people who accepted John but not Jesus.
options.note: They rejected both, calling John demon-possessed and Jesus a glutton.

options.text: As a repentant people awaiting the kingdom.
options.note: They were unrepentant, dismissing both messengers.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus pronounce woe on Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum?

options.text: Because they saw most of His miracles yet did not repent.
options.note: Verse 20 states the reason: great exposure to His works without repentance.

options.text: Because they were more wicked than Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom.
options.note: The point is greater light unheeded; Jesus says pagan cities would have repented, heightening their guilt.

options.text: Because they had rejected the law of Moses.
options.note: Their guilt was refusing to repent despite witnessing His miracles, not rejecting Moses specifically.

options.text: Because they had never heard His teaching.
options.note: They had abundant exposure to His works and words; that is why the woe is so severe.

quiz.q: What does Jesus reveal about Himself in the invitation to the weary?

options.text: That He is gentle and humble in heart, giving rest and an easy yoke to those who come.
options.note: Verses 28-30 reveal His tender heart and the rest He offers.

options.text: That He offers rest only to those who first prove themselves worthy.
options.note: He invites all who are weary and burdened; the rest is a gift to the needy, not a reward for the worthy.

options.text: That His demands are as heavy as the law of the scribes.
options.note: He says His yoke is easy and His burden light, unlike the crushing yoke of the scribes.

options.text: That He welcomes only the wise and learned.
options.note: The Father reveals these things to little children, and Jesus welcomes the weary, not the self-sufficient.

questions: Even John the Baptist wrestled with doubt when Jesus did not act as he expected. How does Jesus' gentle answer to John encourage you to bring your own honest questions to Him?
This generation rejected both John's severity and Jesus' warmth, criticizing whatever came. Where might you be finding excuses to keep Jesus at arm's length rather than responding to Him?
The cities that saw the most miracles faced the greatest judgment for not repenting. How much light have you been given, and how are you responding to it?
Jesus said the Father reveals Himself to little children, not the self-sufficient wise. What would it look like to come to God in childlike humility rather than self-reliance?
Jesus describes His own heart as gentle and humble and invites the weary to rest. What burden are you carrying, and what would it mean to bring it to Him and take His easy yoke this week?

translationNotes.note: Does not fall away on account of Me may also be rendered is not offended by Me; Jesus blesses those who do not stumble over His unexpected way of being Messiah.

Subject to violence, and the violent lay claim to it, may also be rendered has been forcefully advancing, and the forceful lay hold of it; the saying is notably difficult and read both as opposition and as forceful advance.
He is the Elijah who was to come identifies John with the promised Elijah of Malachi 4:5, fulfilling the forerunner role in spirit and mission.
